parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man calls a railway lost property office about a bag he left on a train.
script: Lost property office, how can I help?
Hello. I left a bag on a train this morning, and I'm hoping someone handed it in.
I'll take the details. Can I have your name?
Leo Brandt. The surname is B, R, A, N, D, T.
Thank you. What kind of bag is it?
It's a backpack. Not a big one.
Green. Dark green. Lots of people think it's black, but it's definitely green.
The eight fifteen from Oxford. It arrived here at about nine thirty.
Yes, carriage six. I was sitting near the door.
The most important thing is my laptop. There was also a book about birds, which I'd borrowed from the library, so I really need that back too.
Is there anything that would help us identify the bag?
Yes. There's a small badge on the front pocket, from a music festival.
That's helpful. What's the best time to contact you?
I'm in meetings most of the day, so any time after four p.m., please.
Fine. If we find it, you can collect it from this office. There's a small handling fee of three pounds.
No problem at all. Thank you.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: An organiser talks about this year's food festival.
script: Hi everyone, I'm Sam Patel, one of the organisers of the Harbour Food Festival. I'd like to tell you a bit about what's happening this year.

The festival began in 2015 with just twelve stalls in the town square. This year we have over a hundred, and because of that we've moved the whole event to the harbour front, where there's much more space.

There's one completely new feature this year, which we're very excited about: a cooking competition for children aged eight to twelve. We've had music in the evenings for a few years now, so that's not new.
We're also trying to reduce waste, so we're asking all visitors to bring their own cups and containers. Most stalls will give you a small discount if you do.

Let me run through the programme. On Friday, things start quietly. There's a cheese tasting in the afternoon, and in the evening a vegan baking workshop, and then live music on the main stage until late.
Saturday is our busiest day. The highlight is a cookery demonstration by a famous television chef, which takes place at midday.
And on Sunday, we finish with the children's cooking competition in the morning, and a big seafood barbecue on the beach in the afternoon.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Mia and Kofi, discuss a presentation about energy for a small island.
script: Mia, let's finalise our presentation on energy options for the island community.
Sure. I think we should start by explaining why the island needs to change. At the moment, all its electricity comes from diesel, which has to be shipped in.
And that's expensive. But actually, I think the strongest argument is reliability. When storms stop the ferries, the island can run out of fuel.
Good point. Let's lead with that.
How long do we have for the presentation?
Fifteen minutes, plus five for questions. So we can't go into much technical detail.
What did you make of the interview with the island's council leader?
I was surprised. I thought she'd be worried about cost, but her main concern was making sure local people own the energy projects.
Should we recommend just one energy source?
I don't think so. A combination is safer, so if one fails, the others can still supply power.
OK. Let's go through what we've found about each one. Solar panels are definitely the cheapest to install.
Yes, but they need a large area of land, and land is limited on the island.
Wind turbines produce a lot of power, but residents on another island complained they were noisy.
And there's some concern that they harm seabirds, which matters because the island has important bird colonies.
Then there's tidal power. It's expensive to build, but it's the most reliable, because tides are completely predictable.

parts.title: Part 4
script: Good afternoon. Today's topic is language endangerment, and what can be done about it.
There are around seven thousand languages spoken in the world today. However, many of them have very few speakers, and linguists estimate that about half could disappear by the end of this century.

How does a language die? Usually not suddenly. A language becomes endangered when children stop speaking it, often because parents believe another language will give them better opportunities. Once a generation grows up without it, the language can disappear within a lifetime.

But decline is not always permanent. The most famous example of revival is Hebrew. For centuries it was used mainly for religious purposes. In the late nineteenth century, Eliezer Ben-Yehuda insisted on speaking only Hebrew at home, and his son became the first native speaker of modern Hebrew. Today it has millions of speakers.
Welsh offers another example. After a long decline, the number of young Welsh speakers is rising, largely thanks to schools that teach all subjects in Welsh.
In New Zealand, the Maori community created language nests: pre-schools where young children are surrounded by the Maori language from an early age.
Technology is also helping. There are now apps for learning many small languages, and young people are using them on social media, which makes the languages feel modern rather than old-fashioned.
Even where revival is unlikely, linguists work with elderly speakers to produce dictionaries and grammars, so that the language is at least documented.

Why does all this matter? Because a language contains knowledge. Many indigenous languages, for example, have detailed words for local plants and their uses, which may be lost forever. Ultimately, though, no outside expert can save a language. Revival depends on the commitment of the community itself.

passages.title: The Dabbawalas of Mumbai
paragraphs: Every working day in Mumbai, thousands of office workers sit down to a hot, home-cooked lunch that was prepared in their own kitchens only a few hours earlier. The meals are delivered by the city's dabbawalas, a network of around 5,000 delivery workers who carry an estimated 200,000 lunchboxes across the city each day. The service was started in 1890 by a man called Mahadeo Havaji Bachche, and it has continued, with remarkably few changes, for more than a century.

The system works in stages. In the late morning, a dabbawala collects lunchboxes from homes in his area and takes them by bicycle to the nearest railway station. There the boxes are sorted and loaded onto suburban trains, often in special luggage compartments. At stations in the business districts, they are sorted again and handed to other dabbawalas, who deliver them to offices in time for lunch. In the afternoon, the process runs in reverse, and the empty boxes are returned home.

What makes this possible is a simple code painted on the lid of each box. Using a combination of colours, numbers and symbols, it indicates where the box was collected, which station it must go to, and the building and floor where it should be delivered. The code is easy to read even for workers with little formal education, and many dabbawalas never went beyond primary school.

The service has a reputation for extraordinary accuracy. A figure often repeated in business magazines claims that only one box in sixteen million goes astray. The figure has never been independently verified, and some researchers doubt it, but customers generally agree that mistakes are very rare.

The organisation is also unusual in its structure. The dabbawalas operate as a cooperative, in which every member is a shareholder and earns roughly the same monthly income. Decisions are made by elected leaders, and there is a strong sense of discipline: workers who arrive late or drink alcohol at work can be fined.

In recent decades, the dabbawalas have become famous far beyond Mumbai. Prince Charles visited them in 2003, and business schools around the world have studied the system as an example of efficient logistics without advanced technology. The COVID-19 pandemic was a severe blow, as offices closed and demand collapsed. Since then the service has adapted, and customers can now book deliveries through an app, although the basic method of delivery remains unchanged.

passages.title: Losing the Dark
paragraphs: For most of human history, a clear night revealed thousands of stars and the pale band of the Milky Way. Today, that sight has become rare. A global atlas published in 2016 estimated that around 80 percent of the world's population lives under skies polluted by artificial light, and that the Milky Way is hidden from about a third of humanity, including most people in Europe and North America.

The consequences for wildlife can be severe. Sea turtle hatchlings emerge from their nests at night and find the ocean by moving towards the brightest horizon, which is normally the moonlit sea. Near brightly lit beaches, many crawl inland instead and die. Migrating birds, which navigate partly by the stars, can become confused by city lights and collide with buildings, and huge numbers of insects die circling street lamps, with knock-on effects for the animals that feed on them.

Humans are affected too. Our bodies run on a daily cycle controlled partly by light. Darkness triggers the release of melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate sleep. Exposure to bright light at night suppresses this hormone, and several studies have linked artificial light at night to sleep problems and other health issues, although the evidence on long-term effects is still developing.

Astronomers were among the first to raise the alarm. As cities grew, observatories that had once enjoyed dark skies found their views increasingly washed out. Many major telescopes are now located in remote places, such as the deserts of northern Chile, partly to escape artificial light.

Many people hoped that the switch to LED street lighting would ease the problem, since LEDs are efficient and can be directed precisely. In practice, the opposite has often happened. Because LEDs are cheap to run, cities have installed more of them and made them brighter. Many also produce a cold, bluish light that scatters more in the atmosphere. A citizen-science study published in 2023, based on thousands of observations by members of the public, found that the night sky was brightening by nearly 10 percent a year, much faster than satellite measurements had suggested, partly because satellites cannot detect much blue light.

Unlike many environmental problems, light pollution is relatively simple and cheap to fix. Lights can be shielded so that they point downwards rather than into the sky, switched to warmer colours, and dimmed or turned off when they are not needed. In 2001, Flagstaff in Arizona became the first city to be recognised for its efforts to protect the night sky, and a growing number of national parks and rural areas have been designated as dark-sky reserves.

passages.title: Lucky Accidents
paragraphs: The history of science is full of happy accidents. In 1928 Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find that a mould had contaminated one of his dishes of bacteria, and that the bacteria around it had died. In 1945 the engineer Percy Spencer, working on radar equipment, noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted, an observation that led to the microwave oven. In 1968 Spencer Silver, a chemist trying to develop a super-strong adhesive, produced instead a weak glue that could be stuck and unstuck repeatedly; years later it became the basis of the Post-it note.

Stories like these are popular because they suggest that great discoveries can happen to anyone. In my view, this is misleading. The French scientist Louis Pasteur famously remarked that chance favours the prepared mind, and the examples above support him. Countless people must have seen mould on a dish or felt chocolate melt; what mattered was that Fleming and Spencer had the knowledge to recognise that something unusual had happened, and the curiosity to investigate it.

It is also worth remembering how much work followed the moment of luck. Fleming recognised that the mould produced a substance that killed bacteria, but he was unable to purify it in useful quantities and eventually moved on to other research. It was not until 1940 that Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, at Oxford, developed penicillin into a practical drug. Similarly, Silver's glue was regarded as a failure for several years, until a colleague, Art Fry, realised that it was perfect for bookmarks that would not fall out of his hymn book.

Why does this matter today? Because the way research is funded may be squeezing out the conditions in which such discoveries occur. Scientists applying for grants are usually required to state in advance what they expect to find and how their work will be useful. This encourages projects with predictable outcomes and discourages researchers from following unexpected results. I believe that a system which demands to know the answer before the question has been explored leaves too little room for genuine discovery.

This is not an argument against planned research. Most scientific progress comes from careful, systematic work towards defined goals, and the development of vaccines and new materials depends on it. Unexpected discoveries are not more valuable than planned ones; the point is that both are needed, and that a healthy research system should make space for each.

Some organisations have tried to do this. A few funding bodies now set aside money for open-ended research, allowing scientists to pursue questions purely out of curiosity, and some companies give employees time to work on projects of their own choosing. Such schemes are small, but they recognise something that the history of science makes clear: we cannot plan for luck, but we can make it more likely that, when it arrives, someone will notice.

task1.text: The table below shows sales of new cars by type, in thousands, in one country in 2015, 2020 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The table compares sales of petrol, diesel, hybrid and electric cars in one country in 2015, 2020 and 2025.

Overall, sales of conventional petrol and diesel cars fell considerably over the period, while hybrid and electric cars became much more popular. By 2025, electric cars had overtaken diesel and hybrid models and were close to petrol in sales.
In 2015, petrol cars dominated the market with 1.2 million sales, followed by diesel cars at 900,000. Hybrid and electric vehicles were insignificant, at just 60,000 and 10,000 respectively.

Over the next decade, diesel sales collapsed, halving to 450,000 by 2020 and falling to only 150,000 in 2025. Petrol sales declined more gradually, to 700,000. In contrast, hybrid sales rose eightfold to 480,000, and electric car sales grew dramatically, from 10,000 to 520,000, making them the second most popular type by the end of the period.

task2.text: Some people believe that museums and art galleries should be free for everyone to visit. Others think that visitors should pay an entrance fee. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: Museums and galleries hold some of a nation's most valuable cultural treasures, and there is ongoing debate about whether the public should pay to see them. While entrance fees can help these institutions survive, I believe that free entry, at least to permanent collections, is the better policy.

Those who support charging argue that museums are expensive to run. Buildings must be maintained, collections protected and staff paid, and governments often cannot cover all these costs. Entrance fees provide a reliable source of income and may also mean that people who actually use museums contribute more than those who do not. Furthermore, some suggest that visitors value an experience more highly when they have paid for it.

On the other hand, free entry has clear social benefits. When the United Kingdom abolished charges at its national museums in 2001, visitor numbers rose dramatically, and many of the new visitors came from groups that rarely visited museums before. Fees, even small ones, discourage families on low incomes, students and people who simply want to drop in for half an hour. If museums exist to educate and inspire the whole population, they should not be accessible only to those who can afford them.

In my opinion, a balanced approach is best. Permanent collections should be free, funded by government and private donations, while museums could charge for special temporary exhibitions and earn money from shops and cafés. This protects public access while still generating income.
In conclusion, although entrance fees can help with funding, I believe the educational and social value of museums is greatest when everyone can visit them freely.

speaking.cue:
Describe a website or app that you use often.
You should say:
- what it is
- how you found out about it
- what you use it for
and explain why it is useful to you.
speaking.cueModel: The app I'd like to talk about is a note-taking app called Notion, which I use almost every day. I first heard about it from a senior student at university, who showed me how she organised all her course materials in it, and I was impressed by how tidy everything looked. At first, I found it a bit confusing, because you can do so many things with it, but after watching a few tutorials I got the hang of it. Now I use it for pretty much everything. I keep my lecture notes there, I plan my week with a simple to-do list, and I also use it to track my IELTS preparation, for example by writing down new vocabulary and the mistakes I make in practice tests. The main reason it's so useful is that everything is in one place and it works on both my laptop and my phone, so I can check my notes on the bus. It's also helped me become much more organised. Before, I used to have bits of paper everywhere and I'd often forget deadlines, but that hardly ever happens now.
